drills.q: State the exact single-term difference between the SARSA and Q-learning update rules.
drills.a: SARSA's target uses Q(s',a') for the action a' actually sampled from the behavior policy; Q-learning's target uses max_a' Q(s',a'), the best possible next action, regardless of what the behavior policy will actually do next.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why Q-learning learns the cliff-edge path but SARSA learns a safer path on cliff walking.
drills.a: Q-learning's target always uses max_a' Q(s',a'), so cliff-adjacent states are valued as if the agent always acts optimally afterward, ignoring its own exploration risk -- making the risky edge look good. SARSA's target uses the actually-sampled a' from the epsilon-greedy policy, so the epsilon-probability of an accidental fall (and its -100 cost) is baked into the value of cliff-adjacent states, pulling them down and pushing the learned policy away from the edge.

drills.q: A colleague claims Q-learning is strictly better than SARSA because it learns the optimal policy. Push back on this.
drills.a: Q-learning's converged Q-table does represent the optimal deterministic policy's values, but that conflates the eventual answer with the training-time process -- Q-learning's training-time behavior is riskier because it doesn't account for its own exploration. Whether it's 'better' depends on whether the training process itself has real consequences; if so, SARSA is the correct choice.

drills.q: Why does Q-learning's off-policy property enable experience replay while vanilla SARSA's on-policy property makes naive replay invalid?
drills.a: Q-learning's target depends only on (s,a,r,s'), independent of which policy generated the data or would act next -- old transitions remain valid. SARSA's target explicitly needs a', the action the CURRENT behavior policy would take; a replayed transition's recorded a' is stale, from a possibly very different old policy, violating the on-policy assumption the update relies on.

drills.q: Your Q-table has stopped changing (converged) for all observed states, but performance is still poor on rare edge cases. Does this contradict Watkins & Dayan's convergence proof?
drills.a: No -- the proof requires every (s,a) pair to be visited infinitely often. If rare edge-case states are under-visited by the exploration policy, the proof simply doesn't apply to them; a converged-looking table can have arbitrarily wrong values there. This is a coverage problem, not a violation of the theorem.

drills.q: Design the algorithm choice and training setup for a real warehouse robot learning to navigate near a physically hazardous zone.
drills.a: Use SARSA (or Expected SARSA for lower variance) since training-time behavior has real physical consequences and Q-learning would keep executing risky near-hazard trajectories throughout exploration. Also: hand-constrain the action set near the hazard, decay epsilon over training (GLIE schedule), and train substantially in simulation first -- while noting that sim-to-real gap remains a separate risk regardless of the tabular algorithm chosen.
